title: Digital PR, Brand Mentions & E-E-A-T
subtitle: Earn coverage, build a recognized brand entity, show up accurately in AI answers, and demonstrate experience, expertise and trust
description:
Search engines and AI answer engines increasingly reward brands that are **recognized, cited and trusted**. This advanced course shows you how to build that recognition through digital PR and brand authority work — ethically and measurably.

You will learn how journalists judge newsworthiness, run a repeatable campaign process, and build data-led campaigns from public data and surveys with a reproducible Python workflow. We cover press releases versus pitches, reactive PR, and a current playbook for journalist request platforms including the relaunched HARO, Qwoted and Featured. We then turn to trust: thought leadership, compliant reviews under Google's rules, the US FTC reviews rule and the UK DMCC Act; entity signals, E-E-A-T and author pages; knowledge panels; and how to measure and improve brand mentions in AI search and LLM answers. Finally, you will measure PR with a balanced scorecard aligned with Barcelona Principles 4.0 and build AI-assisted PR workflows with human QA. Examples draw on the UK, US, UAE, KSA and Pakistan.

Build thought leadership and compliant review programs under platform rules and consumer law
Strengthen entity signals, E-E-A-T, author pages and knowledge panels
Measure and improve brand mentions and citations in AI search and LLM answers

lessons.title: What makes a story newsworthy
lessons.body:
### Digital PR in one sentence

Digital PR earns **coverage, links, mentions and brand authority** by giving journalists stories their readers want. Unlike link building outreach, the "customer" is a newsroom working to deadlines with its own editorial standards. Your job is to think like an editor.

### The news values

Journalism schools teach variations of the same list. A story needs at least two of these to have a chance:

| News value | Question an editor asks | Example angle |
|---|---|---|
| **Timeliness** | Why now? | New data released the week a regulation takes effect |
| **Proximity** | Why does this matter to *our* readers? | City-by-city rankings; "Karachi vs Lahore" comparisons |
| **Impact** | How many people does it affect, and how much? | Cost-of-living, salaries, rents, bills |
| **Novelty** | Is this new or surprising? | First-ever data on an emerging behavior |
| **Conflict / tension** | Is there a debate or contrast? | Remote vs office; generational differences |
| **Human interest** | Is there a person or emotion at the heart of it? | Founder story, customer transformation |
| **Prominence** | Does it involve a well-known person, place or brand? | Analysis of a famous event's ripple effects |
| **Usefulness** | Will readers act on it? | Practical guide tied to a deadline (tax, school admissions) |

### Hooks: connecting your expertise to the news

A **hook** is the reason a journalist would publish now. Common hooks:

- **Calendar moments**: Ramadan, Eid, Diwali, Christmas, Black Friday, back-to-school, tax deadlines, budget announcements, national days (UAE National Day, Saudi National Day, Pakistan Independence Day).
- **News events**: regulation changes, platform updates, economic data releases.
- **Trends**: rising search interest, social conversations.
- **Anniversaries**: "five years since...".
- **Data releases**: your own proprietary data or new analysis of public data.

### Reactive vs proactive PR

- **Reactive (newsjacking)**: respond quickly to breaking news with expert comment or rapid data. Speed matters — hours, not days. Requires experts on standby and pre-approved sign-off processes.
- **Proactive**: planned campaigns with original data, creative assets or stories, launched on a chosen date. Longer shelf life, more links, more effort.

Healthy programs run both: reactive work keeps relationships warm; proactive campaigns deliver big moments.

### Campaign formats that tend to work

1. **Data studies and indexes** — "The most affordable cities for freelancers", using public data plus your analysis.
2. **Surveys** — opinions or behaviors of a defined group (with rigorous methodology).
3. **Proprietary data insights** — anonymized, aggregated data from your platform (with privacy safeguards).
4. **Tools and interactive experiences** — calculators, quizzes, maps that journalists can reference.
5. **Expert guides tied to a moment** — "How to protect your home during a sandstorm" from a property maintenance firm.
6. **Creative visual campaigns** — reimagined maps, illustrations, visualizations.

### The "so what?" test

For every idea, write the headline a journalist might use. Then ask: *would I click this if I were not in the industry?* If the headline only interests your marketing team ("Company X launches new feature"), it is not news for consumer or business media — though it might suit trade press.

```text
Weak:   "Optimize All releases 2026 SEO report"
Better: "Half of small business websites in the UAE still can't be found for their own
         brand name, study finds"   ← only if your data genuinely shows this
```

The second headline has impact, proximity and surprise — but **only publish claims your data supports**. Fabricated or exaggerated findings damage your reputation with journalists permanently and can breach advertising and consumer protection rules.

### Relevance to the brand

A campaign must connect to what the brand does, or the links and mentions will not help its authority on relevant topics. A tire retailer running a celebrity-baby-names study may win coverage but builds little topical authority. Aim for the overlap between **what journalists want**, **what your audience cares about**, and **what you are credible on**.

### Common mistakes

- Pitching company news as if it were consumer news.
- Ignoring timing — the best idea launched in a crowded news week sinks.
- Stretching data to fit a headline.
- Campaigns with no connection to the brand's expertise.

### Why newsworthiness matters even more in the AI-search era

Coverage in reputable publications does more than send referral traffic. It is how independent sources come to describe your brand, and those descriptions feed the way search engines and AI answer engines understand who you are and what you're credible on (Module 4 covers this in depth). A story that journalists genuinely want to run earns mentions in exactly the kinds of sources that matter. A story that only your marketing team loves earns nothing.

### Hands-on: the idea scoring sheet

Score every idea before anyone builds anything. Use a shared spreadsheet with one row per idea:

```text
Idea | Draft headline (as a journalist would write it) | Timeliness | Proximity | Impact | Novelty | Conflict | Human interest | Usefulness | Brand relevance (0-3) | Credibility (0-3) | News score | Total
```

Score each news value 0 (absent), 1 (present) or 2 (strong). Then use formulas so brand fit can't be ignored:

```text
News score (column L):   =SUM(C2:I2)
Total (column M):        =IF(OR(J2=0, K2=0), 0, L2 * (J2 + K2))
```

An idea with zero brand relevance or zero credibility scores zero overall, however exciting it is. That rule stops "celebrity baby names" campaigns for tire retailers before they start.

### Hands-on: pressure-test headlines with an AI assistant

AI assistants are useful sparring partners for ideation — they are fast at generating angles and at playing a skeptical editor. They are not a source of facts or data.

```text
You are a skeptical news editor at <publication type, e.g., a UAE business news site>.
Here are 10 draft headlines for data stories from <brand, what it does>.
For each: (1) which news values it has, (2) the first question you'd ask the PR person,
(3) whether you'd run it, commission a different angle, or bin it — and why.
Do not invent data or assume findings. Be blunt.
HEADLINES:
<paste>
```

Use the feedback to sharpen angles, then validate them against real coverage (search recent news for similar stories) and real data.

### Trade press versus consumer press

Company news that fails the "so what?" test for national media can still be excellent for trade publications, which cover product launches, hires and partnerships in their sector. Match the story to the outlet: a new logistics integration may be news in a logistics trade title and meaningless to a lifestyle desk.

### How to measure success

Track, per idea: whether it passed scoring, whether it launched, coverage by tier, links and brand mentions earned, and — over time — which news values and formats consistently win in your niche. Your scoring sheet becomes more accurate as you add results.

lessons.title: From ideation to launch: running a campaign
lessons.body:
### A repeatable campaign process

Successful digital PR teams do not rely on inspiration. They run a process that turns many ideas into a few strong, validated campaigns.

### Stage 1: Ideation

- **Inputs**: brand expertise, audience questions (from search data, sales calls, social), calendar moments, recent coverage in target publications, public datasets.
- **Session format**: 45 minutes, diverse participants, quantity first. Use prompts: "What does our data know that nobody else does?", "What do people in [city] argue about?", "What would change if [trend] continued?"
- Aim for 30+ rough ideas.

### Stage 2: Validation

Score each idea from 1 to 5:

| Criterion | Question |
|---|---|
| News value | Which news values does it hit? |
| Brand relevance | Are we credible here? |
| Data feasibility | Can we get robust data quickly and ethically? |
| Target media fit | Can we name ten journalists who cover this? |
| Link potential | Will coverage naturally link (e.g. to a tool, full data, methodology)? |
| Risk | Could it offend, mislead or backfire? |

**Pre-validation trick:** search news for similar stories in the past two years. If similar campaigns got coverage, the topic has appetite; if identical ones exist, find a new angle (localization, update, different dataset).

### Stage 3: Data and methodology

- **Public data**: government statistics (e.g. the UK Office for National Statistics, US Census Bureau, Pakistan Bureau of Statistics, UAE and Saudi statistics authorities), open data portals, academic sources. Cite them precisely.
- **Surveys**: reputable panel providers, clear sampling, neutral wording, adequate sample sizes for any sub-group you plan to report.
- **Proprietary data**: aggregated and anonymized, with legal/privacy review.

Write the methodology *before* analyzing, to avoid cherry-picking. Keep an audit trail of calculations — journalists and fact-checkers may ask.

### Stage 4: Asset creation

The landing page on your site is the **link target**. Include:

- A headline and short summary of key findings.
- Data tables and charts (downloadable, with source lines).
- Methodology section.
- Expert commentary with a named, credentialed spokesperson.
- Localized cuts (by city, country, age group) — each is a separate story for regional media.
- Press contact details.

Make the page fast, mobile-friendly and crawlable. Link from it to relevant service or product pages where helpful.

### Stage 5: Sell-in (pitching)

- Build a **media list** by beat: journalists who have covered similar stories recently. Personal, relevant, verified.
- Write **tailored pitches** by segment — national consumer, business, regional, trade — each leading with the angle that suits them (Module 2 covers pitch craft).
- Consider an **exclusive** with one top-tier outlet, then a wider release once it runs.
- Pitch **early in the day and early in the week** in the journalist's time zone (UAE and KSA newsrooms, UK and US timings differ; Friday/Saturday weekends apply in some Gulf media).

### Stage 6: Launch and follow-through

- Monitor coverage with alerts and media monitoring.
- Reply to journalist questions within the hour.
- Ask for links politely when coverage uses your data without one (link to the methodology is a reasonable request).
- Share coverage on owned channels.

### Stage 7: Review

Within two weeks: coverage count and quality, links (followed/nofollow), referral traffic, brand search change, lessons learned. A campaign that underperforms often succeeds with a second round of localized or re-angled pitching.

### Ethics and risk review

Before launch, run a short risk review:

- Could the data be misinterpreted or misused?
- Does the campaign stereotype a group, city or nationality?
- Is it sensitive in any market (religious, political or cultural context in the Gulf, South Asia, UK or US)?
- Is anything presented as fact that is actually opinion or estimate?
- Does any claim need legal or compliance sign-off (financial, health)?

### Illustrative example

A Karachi-based fintech analyzes anonymized, aggregated transaction patterns (with legal sign-off) and public inflation data to publish a "cost of a school term" index for major Pakistani cities ahead of the new academic year. It pitches national business desks with the headline figures, regional outlets with city cuts, and parenting bloggers with a savings guide. The landing page includes a calculator and methodology, so coverage links naturally. (Illustrative scenario; outcomes vary.)

### Common mistakes

- Skipping validation and building the first idea.
- Landing pages that bury the data or gate it behind a form.
- Pitching everyone the same angle.
- Launching on a day dominated by major breaking news without a plan to pause.

### Hands-on: build a campaign tracker and media list

Run each campaign from one shared tracker. A spreadsheet or Airtable base works; the columns matter more than the tool.

```text
MEDIA LIST (one row per journalist)
Name | Outlet | Tier (1-3) | Beat | Recent relevant article (link + date) | Angle for them | Region/time zone |
Language | Contact route (email/LinkedIn/X) | Pitched (date) | Follow-up (date) | Response | Coverage link | Link? (followed/nofollow/none)
```

Rules that keep lists healthy:

1. **Every row needs a recent relevant article.** If you can't find one from the last few months, the journalist probably isn't right for this story.
2. **One angle per segment.** National consumer, business, regional and trade each get a different lead.
3. **Respect privacy and platform rules.** Use professional contact details journalists publish for work, keep lists secure, honor opt-outs immediately, and follow applicable data-protection and anti-spam laws (for example, UK GDPR and PECR in the UK, GDPR in the EU).

### Launch-day checklist

```text
T-7 days   Landing page live but unlinked (noindex off, crawlable), methodology and data downloads checked
T-5        Exclusive offered to one top-tier outlet (if using), with clear terms and embargo time zone
T-3        Spokesperson briefed; media Q&A and approved quotes ready; images and charts exported
T-1        Pitches scheduled for each segment's local morning; monitoring alerts set up
T-0        Send; reply to questions within the hour; log coverage as it lands
T+2        Follow-up once, with a new angle or local cut — not "just checking in"
T+14       Review: coverage by tier, links, referral traffic, branded search, lessons
```

### Monitoring coverage

Set up Google Alerts for the campaign name, headline figures and brand name, and use your media-monitoring or backlink tool to catch coverage that doesn't link. In Arabic and Urdu media, supplement with manual searches — some tools cover these languages poorly.

### How to measure success

At T+14, compare results with the targets you set before launch: pieces of coverage by tier, new linking domains (and followed versus nofollow), referral sessions and conversions, and whether key messages and the spokesperson appeared. Record what you'd change for the next campaign.

video.script: Great digital PR looks spontaneous from the outside. Inside, it's a process. It starts with ideation. Gather your brand's expertise, your audience's questions, the calendar of moments like Ramadan, back-to-school or budget day, and public data sources. Then generate lots of ideas, thirty or more, without judging them. Next, validate. Score each idea on news value, brand relevance, data feasibility, media fit, link potential and risk. Check whether similar stories have been covered before. If they have, the topic has appetite. Find your fresh angle. Then the data. Write your methodology before you analyze anything, so you're not tempted to cherry-pick. Use credible public sources, reputable survey panels, or anonymized data from your own platform with legal sign-off. Build a landing page that deserves the link: key findings, charts people can download, the methodology, a named expert, and local breakdowns for regional media. When you pitch, tailor the angle. National, business, regional and trade journalists want different stories from the same data. Before you launch, pause for a risk review. Could this be misread? Does it stereotype anyone? Is it sensitive in any of your markets? And after launch, respond to journalists fast, ask politely for links where your data is used, and review what worked. The process is what makes success repeatable.

scenes.narration: Most digital PR campaigns that fail don't fail at the pitch. They fail weeks earlier, when someone falls in love with the first idea, skips validation, collects data without a plan, and builds a landing page nobody wants to link to. By the time the pitches go out, the result is already decided. In this lecture, you'll learn a repeatable seven-stage campaign process: ideation, validation, data and methodology, asset creation, sell-in, launch and review. Plus a media list structure and a launch-day checklist you can reuse for every campaign.

lessons.title: Data-led campaigns: original research, surveys and public datasets
lessons.body:
### Why data-led campaigns earn the strongest coverage

Journalists need facts they can't easily produce themselves, and editors love a number that changes how readers see their city, job or wallet. A well-built data campaign gives them a headline figure, local cuts for regional desks, a methodology they can trust and a link target worth citing. Data-led work also ages well: an annual index can earn coverage every year, and each edition strengthens your brand's association with the topic.

The risk is equally clear. A weak sample, a cherry-picked comparison or an AI-invented statistic can end a journalist relationship permanently and may breach advertising and consumer-protection rules. This lesson shows how to do it properly.

### Three sources of data

| Source | Examples | Strengths | Watch-outs |
|---|---|---|---|
| Public data | National statistics offices (UK ONS, US Census Bureau and BLS, Pakistan Bureau of Statistics, UAE's Federal Competitiveness and Statistics Center, Saudi Arabia's General Authority for Statistics), Eurostat, World Bank, OECD, open-data portals, regulators | Credible, free, reproducible | Check licenses and definitions; note release dates; don't compare incompatible measures |
| Surveys | Online panels via reputable research providers | Opinions and behaviors you can't observe otherwise | Sample quality, neutral wording, sub-group sizes, disclosure |
| Proprietary data | Aggregated platform data (bookings, searches, prices) | Unique, hard to copy | Privacy, consent, legal review, commercial sensitivity |

### Survey basics you must get right

- **Define the population** ("UK adults 18+", "UAE residents who shopped online in the past month").
- **Neutral wording.** "How much do you trust online reviews?" not "Do you agree fake reviews are ruining shopping?"
- **Sample size for sub-groups.** If you'll report by city or age group, each group needs enough respondents on its own; small sub-groups produce unstable percentages.
- **Margin of error.** For a simple random sample, the approximate 95% margin of error for a percentage is `1.96 × √(p(1−p)/n)`. With n = 1,000 and p = 50%, that's about ±3.1 percentage points. Online panels are not true random samples, so treat this as a rough guide and don't over-claim small differences.
- **Disclosure.** Publish the sample size, population, dates, method and who commissioned the research. In the UK, members of the British Polling Council and researchers following the Market Research Society Code of Conduct have disclosure obligations; following those norms anywhere builds credibility.

### Hands-on: build a city affordability index with Python and pandas

This example combines two public datasets — median rent and median earnings by city — into a ranked index with a reproducible audit trail. Replace the CSV files with real, properly licensed data and cite the sources.

```python
# pip install pandas
import pandas as pd
from pathlib import Path

RENT = Path("data/median_rent_by_city.csv")         # columns: city, median_monthly_rent
EARN = Path("data/median_earnings_by_city.csv")     # columns: city, median_monthly_earnings

def load(path: Path, cols: list[str]) -> pd.DataFrame:
    if not path.exists():
        raise FileNotFoundError(f"Missing data file: {path}")
    df = pd.read_csv(path)
    missing = set(cols) - set(df.columns)
    if missing:
        raise ValueError(f"{path} is missing columns: {missing}")
    return df[cols]

rent = load(RENT, ["city", "median_monthly_rent"])
earn = load(EARN, ["city", "median_monthly_earnings"])

df = rent.merge(earn, on="city", how="inner", validate="one_to_one")
dropped = set(rent.city) ^ set(earn.city)
if dropped:
    print("Cities without both measures (excluded):", sorted(dropped))

df["rent_to_income_pct"] = (df.median_monthly_rent / df.median_monthly_earnings * 100).round(1)
df["rank_most_affordable"] = df.rent_to_income_pct.rank(method="min").astype(int)
df = df.sort_values("rank_most_affordable")

df.to_csv("output/affordability_index.csv", index=False)        # publish as a download
print(df.head(10).to_string(index=False))
print(f"n cities: {len(df)} | median ratio: {df.rent_to_income_pct.median():.1f}%")
```

Keep the script, the raw files and a short README with sources, download dates and definitions in one folder. That folder is your audit trail when a journalist asks "how did you calculate this?"

### Using AI in data campaigns — safely

- **Good uses:** brainstorming angles, suggesting public datasets to investigate (then verifying them at the source), drafting code you review and test, and writing plain-English summaries of results you've already verified.
- **Never:** let an AI tool "provide" statistics, estimate figures you present as findings, or generate quotes. Language models can produce plausible numbers that don't exist.
- **Label everything.** If a figure is an estimate or projection, say so, with the method.

### Worked example: a Gulf "cost of the Eid wardrobe" index

A fashion marketplace in the UAE combines anonymized, aggregated basket data (with legal sign-off) and public inflation data to estimate the typical cost of an Eid outfit in several Gulf cities, with a clear methodology and the sample period. Regional desks receive city cuts, lifestyle writers get a "how to shop smart" guide, and the landing page offers the full table as a download. The pre-launch review removes a comparison by nationality that could have stereotyped groups. (Illustrative scenario.)

### How to measure success

Beyond coverage and links, track how often your figures are cited accurately (with the correct number and attribution), whether outlets link to the methodology, and whether the index earns repeat coverage in later editions. Those are signs of genuine authority.

scenes.narration: Now the margin of error, which trips up many campaigns. And online panels aren't true random samples, so treat the formula as a rough guide, and never over-claim small differences.

lessons.title: Press releases vs pitches
lessons.body:
### Two different tools

| | Press release | Pitch |
|---|---|---|
| What | Formal, complete announcement in news style | Short, personal email proposing a story angle |
| Audience | Many outlets, newswires, your newsroom page | One journalist or a small segment |
| Best for | Official company news, financial results, major launches, regulated disclosures | Data stories, expert commentary, features, exclusives |
| SEO value | Wire-distributed releases produce mostly nofollow, syndicated copies; value is exposure | Earned editorial coverage and links when journalists use it |

A common misconception is that distributing a press release through a wire service "builds links". Syndicated release pages are typically nofollowed or not indexed, and Google has long treated links in widely distributed releases as not passing ranking credit. The value of a release is **visibility** — journalists and the public may see it and write original coverage.

### When a press release is the right choice

- Funding rounds, acquisitions, leadership appointments, financial results.
- Official responses where the exact wording matters (legal or crisis statements).
- Regulated sectors that need a public, formal record.
- A major launch where you want a canonical, quotable source on your newsroom page.

### Writing a press release

```text
FOR IMMEDIATE RELEASE   (or: EMBARGOED UNTIL 00:01 GST, March 12, 2026)

Headline: Clear, factual, under ~12 words
Subheadline: One sentence adding the key detail

CITY, Country — Date — Lead paragraph: who, what, when, where, why in 1–2 sentences.

Second paragraph: the most important supporting detail or data.

Quote from a named spokesperson — adds opinion and meaning, not repetition.

Further detail: context, availability, pricing, methodology.

Second quote (optional): partner, customer or expert.

About [Company]: 50–80 words boilerplate.

Media contact: name, email, phone.
###
```

Keep it to one page where possible. Avoid superlatives ("world-leading", "revolutionary") unless you can prove them.

### Embargoes

An embargo allows journalists to prepare a story before a set publication time. Use them for significant data or news, state the time zone clearly, send only to journalists you trust, and never punish a journalist for your own unclear embargo terms.

### Writing a pitch

A pitch is a personal note. Structure:

1. **Subject line = the headline** you imagine them running.
2. **One-line hook**: why this matters to their readers now.
3. **Three bullet findings or key facts** — specific and verifiable.
4. **What you can offer**: full data, expert interview, images, local cuts, exclusive.
5. **Link** to the landing page (no attachments).
6. **Signature** with direct phone number for fast responses.

```text
Subject: Rents in Dubai Marina rose faster than salaries for young professionals, analysis shows

Hi Priya,

With new-year lease renewals under way, our analysis of public rental listings
and salary survey data might be useful for your property coverage:

• [Specific finding 1 with figure from your data]
• [Specific finding 2]
• [Specific finding 3, e.g. neighborhoods where the gap narrowed]

Full data, methodology and city charts: [URL]. Our head of research, Dr. Faisal
Rahman, is available for interview today (Arabic or English).

Best,
Leena | +971 ...
```

*(The subject and findings must reflect your actual analysis.)*

### Exclusives

Offering one outlet an exclusive gives them a reason to prioritize your story. Be clear about what "exclusive" means (first to publish, or only outlet) and for how long. After it runs, pitch the wider media with a new angle.

### Newsroom pages

Maintain a newsroom or press page on your site with releases, media kit, logos, spokesperson bios and contact details. It becomes a source journalists and search engines can reference, and a home for canonical statements.

### Common mistakes

- Using press release wires to "build links".
- Sending the full release as a pitch with no personalization.
- Headlines full of jargon.
- Burying the news in paragraph four.

### Hands-on: turn one announcement into a release and three pitches

Take a real announcement (a funding round, a new data report, a partnership) and produce four pieces from one fact sheet. Start with the facts, not the prose:

```text
FACT SHEET
What happened (one sentence, no adjectives): ________________________________
Date/time and time zone (embargo if any): __________________________________
Numbers (each with source): ________________________________________________
Who is quoted (name, title, one sentence of genuine opinion): _______________
Why it matters to (a) customers (b) the industry (c) a local community: _____
Assets: images (with credits), charts, data download, landing page URL: _____
Media contact (name, direct phone, email, hours): ___________________________
```

Then write:

1. **The press release** for your newsroom page and, if appropriate, a wire service (for visibility, not links).
2. **A trade pitch** leading with what the news means for the sector.
3. **A regional pitch** leading with the local angle (jobs, customers, city data).
4. **A business-desk pitch** leading with the numbers and what they signal.

### Using AI to draft — and what to check

AI assistants can turn a fact sheet into first drafts quickly. Give them only verified facts and tell them not to add any:

```text
Using ONLY the facts below, draft (1) a one-page press release in standard news style and
(2) three pitch emails of under 150 words for: a logistics trade editor, a Riyadh business
reporter, and a UK regional news desk. Subject line = the headline you'd expect them to run.
Do not add numbers, claims, superlatives or quotes that are not in the facts. Mark any gap as [NEED].
FACTS:
<paste fact sheet>
```

Then check every sentence against the fact sheet, rewrite the quotes with the real spokesperson, and personalize each pitch with a reference to the journalist's recent work. Journalists spot generic AI-written pitches quickly, and many ignore them.

### Pitch quality checklist

```text
[ ] Subject line reads like a headline for THEIR outlet
[ ] First sentence says why it matters to their readers now
[ ] Three specific, verifiable facts
[ ] Clear offer (data, interview, images, local cut, exclusive)
[ ] One link, no attachments; direct phone number
[ ] Under ~150 words; personalized reference to their recent coverage
[ ] Embargo terms (if any) stated with time zone
```

### How to measure success

Track open and reply rates by segment and subject line (where your tool allows), coverage per segment, and the ratio of pitches sent to pieces of coverage. A falling ratio usually means better targeting, not just better writing.

lessons.title: Journalist request services and reactive PR
lessons.body:
### Reactive PR: being the source journalists need

Journalists often need expert input fast. Reactive PR means monitoring those needs and responding with useful, credible commentary — often within hours. Done consistently, it builds mentions, links and relationships with modest effort.

### Where requests appear

- **Journalist request platforms**: services such as Qwoted, Featured, Help a B2B Writer, Source of Sources, and in the UK ResponseSource. The landscape changes frequently: HARO, for years the best-known service, was shut down by its owner in late 2024 and later relaunched under new ownership. Check current terms, pricing and quality before committing.
- **Social media hashtags**: #journorequest and #PRrequest on X, and journalist posts on LinkedIn.
- **Direct relationships**: journalists you know emailing you (the best source — see relationship building).
- **Regional communities**: in the Gulf and Pakistan, many journalists source through WhatsApp groups, LinkedIn and industry associations; relationships matter even more.

### Qualifying requests quickly

Respond only when you have **genuine expertise** and can meet the deadline. Check:

1. Is the outlet reputable and relevant to your audience?
2. Does your expert meet the stated criteria (location, credentials, experience)?
3. Can you answer specifically and on time?
4. Is it a genuine journalist request, not a disguised content farm or a "pay to be featured" scheme?

Some "requests" are low-quality sites collecting free content for listicles. They may still be worth it if relevant, but prioritize real publications.

### Writing a strong response

```text
Subject: [Request title] — comment from Sana Malik, Head of E-commerce SEO

Hi Jordan,

Sana Malik, Head of E-commerce SEO at [Company] (12 years in retail search):

"[Direct, specific answer in 2–4 sentences. Include one concrete example or
practical tip. Avoid jargon and self-promotion.]"

"[Optional second point that adds a different angle.]"

Credentials: [one line]. Headshot and bio: [URL to expert page].
Available for a quick call today until 6pm GMT.

Best,
[Name, phone]
```

Principles:

- **Answer the exact question first.** Journalists skim.
- **Be quotable**: short sentences, a clear opinion, a specific example.
- **Do not sell**. No product mentions unless asked.
- **Be accurate**: if you cite a statistic, name the source.
- **Include credentials** and a link to an expert bio page on your site.
- **Speed**: many journalists use the first few good answers.

### Setting up a reactive program

1. **Expert roster**: list each expert, topics, languages, availability and approved bio.
2. **Monitoring rota**: someone checks requests several times a day.
3. **Pre-approved positions**: agree the company's stance on recurring topics so responses do not wait for sign-off.
4. **Response library**: save strong answers to adapt (never paste identical answers across outlets — journalists notice).
5. **Tracking**: log requests answered, published results, links and outlets.

### Newsjacking responsibly

When news breaks in your sector — a Google algorithm update, a new data protection rule, a platform outage — send a short, useful reaction to journalists covering it:

```text
Subject: Comment: what [new rule] means for small online sellers in the UAE

Hi Maryam — if helpful for your coverage of [rule], three practical points for
small sellers from our compliance lead: [1] [2] [3]. Happy to expand by phone.
```

Avoid newsjacking tragedies, disasters or sensitive political events for commercial gain. It damages trust and can cause serious backlash.

### Expectations

Many responses will not be used; that is normal. Some coverage will mention you without a link, or with a nofollow link. Brand mentions in reputable publications still support recognition and trust. Measure over quarters, not weeks.

### Common mistakes

- Answering requests outside your expertise.
- Long, generic answers that bury the insight.
- Sending the same answer to multiple outlets.
- Paying for "guaranteed features" presented as editorial coverage without disclosure.

### Platforms change — see the next lesson

The platform landscape moves quickly. The next lesson, "Journalist request platforms", is a hands-on playbook for HARO (relaunched under Featured.com in 2025), Qwoted, Featured, Source of Sources, ResponseSource and social requests. This lesson focuses on the reactive program behind any platform: monitoring, speed, positions and quality.

### Hands-on: build a rapid-response newsjacking workflow

**1. Monitoring.** Set up alerts for the topics your experts can speak to credibly:

```text
Google Alerts (as-it-happens, results: only the best):
  "Google algorithm update" OR "core update"
  "data protection law" (UAE OR Saudi OR Pakistan)
  "<your sector> regulation" 2026
Google Trends: explore your topics by country; subscribe to trending searches for your market
Social: saved searches on X and LinkedIn for your sector keywords + "journalist" / #journorequest
```

**2. Triage in 15 minutes.** When something breaks, answer three questions in your team chat: Can we add something specific and useful? Is it appropriate to comment (never exploit tragedies)? Who is the right expert, and are they available now?

**3. A 60-minute response template.**

```text
Subject: Comment: what <news> means for <audience> in <market>

Hi <name> — if helpful for your coverage of <news>, three practical points from
<expert name, title> (<one-line credential>):

1. <specific implication>
2. <specific action readers can take>
3. <what to watch next>

<Expert> is available by phone until <time, time zone>. Bio and headshot: <expert page URL>.
<Your name> | <direct phone>
```

**4. Pre-approved positions.** Keep a short document of the company's agreed stance on recurring topics (pricing changes in your sector, regulation, AI use), so responses don't wait for sign-off.

### AI in reactive PR: speed without losing credibility

AI tools can summarize a new regulation, draft a first version of a response from your expert's notes, or check the reading level of a quote. Three rules:

- **The expert's words, not the model's.** Quotes must come from, and be approved by, the named expert.
- **Verify the news itself.** Summaries can misstate details; read the primary source (the regulator's notice, the platform's announcement).
- **Disclose where required.** Some platforms and journalists ask whether AI was used; answer honestly.

### How to measure success

Log every response: time from request or news break to response, outcome (used/not used), outlet tier, link type and topic. Over a quarter, look for faster responses, a rising use rate in your strongest topics, and recurring journalists who come back to your experts directly.

In this lecture, you'll learn where journalist requests appear, how to qualify them quickly, how to write a response journalists actually use, how to build a reactive program with an expert roster and pre-approved positions, and how to newsjack responsibly, with AI speeding you up without costing you credibility.

lessons.title: Journalist request platforms: HARO, Qwoted, Featured and a triage system
lessons.body:
### The landscape in 2026

Journalist request platforms (sometimes called "source request" or "query" services) connect reporters who need expert input with people who can provide it. The market reshaped itself in 2024–2025, so older guides are often wrong. Always check a platform's current terms, pricing and rules before committing time.

| Platform | How it works (at a glance) | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| **HARO (Help a Reporter Out)** | Email digests of journalist queries; sources reply to the reporter | Owned by Cision from 2014; rebranded as Connectively and shut down in December 2024; acquired by Featured.com and relaunched in April 2025 as a free, ad-supported service with several digests a day |
| **Qwoted** | Two-sided marketplace: journalists post requests; experts build profiles and pitch | Free tier and paid plans; strong for business, finance and tech coverage |
| **Featured** (featured.com) | Question-and-answer format: publishers pose questions, experts submit answers, publishers choose which to include | Also HARO's owner since 2025 |
| **Source of Sources (SOS)** | Free email digests of queries, launched by HARO's original founder | Back-to-basics, free |
| **ResponseSource** | UK-based journalist inquiry service (paid, for PR teams and brands) | Strong for UK national, regional and trade media |
| **Help a B2B Writer** | Requests from B2B content writers | Often company blogs and trade content |
| **Social requests** | #journorequest on X; journalist posts on LinkedIn and Bluesky | Free; move fast |

Independent comparisons of these platforms have found relatively little overlap between the requests each one carries, so monitoring two or three relevant services typically surfaces more opportunities than relying on one.

### Quality has become the whole game

Since generative AI became widespread, request platforms have been flooded with generic, AI-written answers. Journalists and platforms have responded by filtering harder; several platforms have introduced rules or checks aimed at low-quality or AI-generated submissions, and journalists increasingly ask for real, verifiable experts. The consequence for you: fewer, better answers from genuine experts outperform mass responses.

### Hands-on: set up a triage system

**1. Route digests into one place.** Create an email label or folder for each platform and a filter that applies it automatically (for example in Gmail: *Settings → Filters*, matching the platform's sending address). Turn off notifications for everything except that folder during your monitoring windows.

**2. Score requests automatically (optional).** If you export or copy requests into a CSV (`platform, outlet, title, deadline, text`), a short script can shortlist the ones that match your experts:

```python
import csv
from datetime import datetime, timezone

EXPERTS = {
    "sana":  {"keywords": ["ecommerce", "e-commerce", "seo", "shopify", "search"], "regions": ["uk", "uae"]},
    "faisal": {"keywords": ["data protection", "privacy", "compliance", "gdpr"],   "regions": ["uae", "saudi", "ksa"]},
}

def score(row: dict) -> tuple[int, str]:
    text = f"{row['title']} {row['text']}".lower()
    best, who = 0, ""
    for name, e in EXPERTS.items():
        s = sum(3 for k in e["keywords"] if k in text) + sum(1 for r in e["regions"] if r in text)
        if s > best:
            best, who = s, name
    return best, who

def hours_left(deadline_iso: str) -> float:
    try:
        dl = datetime.fromisoformat(deadline_iso)
    except ValueError:
        return float("inf")
    if dl.tzinfo is None:
        dl = dl.replace(tzinfo=timezone.utc)
    return (dl - datetime.now(timezone.utc)).total_seconds() / 3600

with open("requests.csv", newline="", encoding="utf-8") as f:
    rows = list(csv.DictReader(f))

shortlist = []
for r in rows:
    s, who = score(r)
    h = hours_left(r.get("deadline", ""))
    if s >= 3 and h > 1:
        shortlist.append((s, round(h, 1), who, r["platform"], r["outlet"], r["title"]))

for item in sorted(shortlist, key=lambda x: (-x[0], x[1])):
    print(item)
```

Keyword matching is crude; a human still decides. The point is to spend your attention on the requests most likely to fit.

**3. Answer with a proven structure.** Use the response template from the previous lesson: answer first, two quotable points, one concrete example, one-line credentials, bio link, call window with time zone.

**4. Log everything.**

```text
Date | Platform | Outlet | Tier | Request title | Expert | Minutes to respond | Used? | Link (followed/nofollow/none) | Notes
```

### Platform etiquette and compliance

- Follow each platform's rules on eligibility, pitching format and follow-ups; breaking them can get an account suspended.
- Don't pay for "guaranteed" editorial placement presented as independent coverage. Paid placements must be clearly disclosed as advertising or sponsorship under advertising rules (for example the FTC's Endorsement Guides in the US and the CAP Code in the UK).
- Links from coverage are the publisher's choice. Many are nofollow or "sponsored"; mentions in reputable outlets still build recognition.
- Never misrepresent credentials or invent experts.

### Worked example: a two-platform routine for a small agency

A three-person agency in Lahore serving UK and Gulf e-commerce clients monitors Qwoted and HARO twice a day, plus #journorequest searches on X. A simple CSV and the triage script shortlist around five requests a day; the team answers two or three with named, credentialed experts. After a quarter, their log shows most wins came from business and e-commerce trade outlets, and that responses sent within an hour were used far more often, so they tighten their monitoring windows. (Illustrative scenario.)

### How to measure success

Use your log to calculate, per platform: responses sent, use rate, average time to respond, share of Tier 1–2 outlets and link types. Drop or de-prioritize platforms that consistently deliver low-relevance outlets, and double down on those that reach your customers.

lessons.body:
### What thought leadership is (and isn't)

Thought leadership is **publicly sharing distinctive, expert perspectives that help your audience think or act better**. It is not generic content with an executive's name on it. Real thought leadership earns speaking invitations, podcast appearances, bylines, citations and, over time, the brand and entity signals that support search visibility.

### The three ingredients

1. **Expertise**: real experience and knowledge — the person has done the work.
2. **A point of view**: a clear, defensible stance ("most small businesses should not start with SEO — here's what to do first").
3. **Evidence**: data, case studies, frameworks and examples that back the view.

### Formats and channels

| Format | Where | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| Bylined articles | Trade and business publications | Pitch ideas to editors; follow their guidelines; links may be nofollow |
| Owned long-form | Your blog or insights hub | The home of your frameworks and data; link target |
| LinkedIn posts and newsletters | Professional audience | Consistency matters; share lessons, not just announcements |
| Speaking | Conferences, meetups, webinars, university lectures | Speaker pages often link; talks create video and quotable content |
| Podcasts | Industry and business shows | Build relationships and reach |
| Research and reports | Owned, promoted via PR | Strongest for citations |
| Video and short-form | YouTube, social platforms | Show the person; builds recognition |

### A thought leadership plan

1. **Choose the people**: two or three genuine experts, not only the CEO.
2. **Define territories**: two or three topics each person can own (e.g. "e-commerce SEO for bilingual Gulf stores").
3. **Develop signature ideas**: a framework, a contrarian insight, an annual data point. Name them — named frameworks are easier to cite.
4. **Create a cadence**: for example, one substantial owned article a month, weekly LinkedIn posts, one pitch for a byline per quarter, speaking submissions twice a year.
5. **Repurpose**: a talk becomes an article, a LinkedIn series, a podcast conversation and a video clip.
6. **Support with author infrastructure**: expert profile pages, consistent bios and headshots across platforms (important for entity and E-E-A-T, covered in Module 4).

### Ghostwriting honestly

Many executives work with writers. That is fine when the ideas, experiences and opinions are genuinely theirs and they review what is published under their name. Publishing AI-generated or ghostwritten content that misrepresents someone's experience undermines trust — and trust is the foundation of the whole strategy.

### Bylines in publications

- Study the publication: tone, length, audience, contributor guidelines.
- Pitch an idea, not a finished article, unless the publication asks for full drafts.
- Offer genuinely useful, non-promotional content.
- Accept the publication's link policy. Many limit contributor links or make them nofollow; a byline's value is audience and credibility.
- Avoid "contributor networks" that sell placements — those can be link schemes.

### Regional considerations

- In the Gulf, bilingual (Arabic and English) thought leadership reaches wider audiences; regional business publications and events such as industry summits are influential.
- In Pakistan, LinkedIn, YouTube and industry associations are strong channels; English and Urdu content can reach different segments.
- In the UK and US, niche trade publications often drive more qualified attention than broad national outlets.

### Measuring thought leadership

- Inbound invitations (speaking, podcasts, commentary requests).
- Coverage and citations of named frameworks or data.
- Growth in branded and person-name searches.
- Engagement quality (comments from target audience, not vanity likes).
- Sales conversations referencing the content.

### Common mistakes

- Publishing opinions without evidence.
- Only the CEO speaks, on every topic.
- Inconsistent bios and names across platforms.
- Paying for "featured expert" placements presented as editorial.

### Contributor content and Google's site reputation abuse policy

Since 2024, Google's spam policies have included **site reputation abuse**: publishing third-party pages on a host site mainly to exploit that site's ranking signals, with little oversight from the host. Google clarified in late 2024 that first-party involvement or a licensing arrangement doesn't exempt such content. For thought leaders this means: write bylines that genuinely serve the publication's readers, under its normal editorial standards. Avoid "contributor" programs that sell placements for search value — they are both a link-scheme and a reputation risk.

### Hands-on: build a signature idea and a 90-day plan

**1. Signature idea worksheet.** Give each expert one idea they can be known for.

```text
SIGNATURE IDEA
Expert: __________________   Territory (2-3 topics): _________________________
The common belief in our industry: ______________________________________________
What our experience/data shows instead: _________________________________________
Evidence we can publish (data, cases, results): __________________________________
Name for the idea (short, memorable, descriptive): _______________________________
Who needs to hear it (audience + publications + events): _________________________
Risks (claims we must support; topics to avoid): _________________________________
```

**2. A 90-day cadence** (adapt the volume to what your experts can sustain):

```text
Weeks 1-2   Owned long-form article introducing the signature idea (with data/examples)
Weekly      2 LinkedIn posts from the expert: lessons, examples, counterpoints (not announcements)
Week 3      Pitch 3 byline ideas to trade publications (idea + outline, not a finished draft)
Week 4      Submit to 2 conference or webinar calls for speakers
Monthly     1 podcast guest pitch; 1 short video explaining the idea
Week 8      Publish a small data point or case study that supports the idea
Week 12     Review: invitations, citations, branded/person searches, sales mentions
```

**3. Ghostwriting and AI, honestly.** Record a 20-minute interview with the expert, transcribe it, and draft from their words. AI can help turn a transcript into an outline or tighten a draft, but the ideas, experiences and opinions must be the expert's, and they must review everything published under their name. Keep a note of what was drafted with AI in case a publication asks — many editors now have policies on AI-assisted submissions.

```text
Prompt: Here is a transcript of an interview with <expert, role>. Draft an 800-word article
outline for <publication>'s readers, using only the ideas, examples and opinions in the transcript.
Quote the expert verbatim where possible. List any claims that need a source as [SOURCE NEEDED].
```

### How to measure success

At 90 days, count inbound invitations (podcasts, events, commentary requests), citations of the named idea, growth in searches for the expert's name and brand (Search Console, and Google Trends for larger brands), engagement from your target audience rather than vanity likes, and sales conversations that mention the content.

lessons.title: Reviews and reputation management
lessons.body:
### Why reviews matter beyond local SEO

Reviews influence purchase decisions, click-through from search results, local rankings (see the Local SEO course), and how both people and systems perceive a brand's trustworthiness. Google's Search Quality Rater Guidelines direct raters to research a website's and creator's reputation using independent sources, including reviews. Reputation is not a single signal you can manipulate; it is what others say about you.

### The rules you must follow

**Platform policies** (Google, Trustpilot, Tripadvisor, app stores and others) generally prohibit:

- **Fake reviews** — written by owners, staff, agencies or paid reviewers.
- **Incentivized reviews** — offering discounts, gifts or payment in exchange for reviews (Google prohibits this for Business Profile reviews).
- **Review gating** — asking only happy customers to review, or filtering customers before sending them to review sites.
- **Conflicts of interest** — employees reviewing their employer, competitors leaving negative reviews.
- **Review suppression** — pressuring customers to remove negative reviews.

**Consumer protection law** increasingly targets fake reviews:

- **US**: the FTC's rule on consumer reviews and testimonials (in force since late 2024) prohibits fake reviews, buying positive or negative reviews, certain insider reviews without disclosure, and review suppression, with civil penalties possible.
- **UK**: the Digital Markets, Competition and Consumers Act 2024 made commissioning, publishing or facilitating fake reviews a banned practice (from April 2025), enforced by the CMA.
- **EU**: consumer rules require businesses to disclose whether and how they verify that reviews come from real customers.
- **Gulf and Pakistan**: consumer protection and cybercrime laws may apply to deceptive practices; seek local advice.

This is general information, not legal advice.

### A compliant review generation system

1. **Ask everyone** — every customer, at the right moment (after delivery, after a successful project milestone).
2. **Make it easy** — a direct link to the review form, QR codes in-store, short request messages.
3. **Use neutral language** — "Would you share your experience?" not "Please leave us 5 stars".
4. **Spread across platforms** relevant to your market (Google, industry sites, Trustpilot, app stores).
5. **Never incentivize** reviews on platforms that forbid it. If you run incentives on your own site (where allowed), disclose them clearly.

```text
Hi Ayesha, thanks for choosing [Business]. We'd really value your honest feedback —
it helps us improve and helps others decide. It takes about a minute: [review link]
```

### Responding to reviews

Respond to reviews — positive and negative — professionally:

- **Positive**: thank them specifically; avoid keyword-stuffed replies.
- **Negative**: acknowledge, apologize where appropriate, avoid arguments or sharing private details, offer an offline route to resolve, and follow up.
- **Fake or policy-violating reviews**: report through the platform's process with evidence; do not accuse the reviewer publicly.

```text
Hi Omar, thank you for the feedback and I'm sorry your order arrived late.
That's not the experience we want for anyone. I've asked our operations lead to
look into it — could you email support@example.com with your order number so
we can put it right? — Nadia, Customer Experience Manager
```

Future customers read responses; calm, helpful replies build trust even on bad reviews.

### Reputation beyond reviews

Monitor your **brand SERP** — what appears when people search your brand name: your site, social profiles, reviews, news, forum threads, complaint sites. Improving it involves:

- Owning and maintaining official profiles (LinkedIn, YouTube, industry directories).
- Earning coverage in reputable publications.
- Addressing legitimate complaints publicly and fixing root causes.
- Publishing clear About, policies and contact pages.
- Legal routes only for genuinely defamatory or unlawful content — not for honest criticism.

### Crisis readiness

Prepare a simple crisis plan: who responds, approval chain, holding statements, and monitoring. In a crisis, speed, honesty and empathy matter more than polished wording.

### Common mistakes

- "Review swaps" with other businesses.
- Buying reviews through agencies that promise "real accounts".
- Responding defensively or revealing customer details.
- Ignoring reviews on niche platforms your audience uses.

### Hands-on: a compliant review program in four steps

**1. Get your direct review links.** In Google Business Profile you can copy a "request reviews" link or QR code from your profile's management options; other platforms (Trustpilot, app stores, industry sites) offer their own invitation methods. Check each platform's invitation rules — some restrict how you may invite or what you may say.

**2. Automate a neutral request to every customer.** Trigger it from your e-commerce, booking or CRM platform at a natural moment (after delivery, after a completed appointment). The same message goes to every customer — no filtering by expected sentiment.

```text
TRIGGER: order status = delivered + 3 days (or appointment = completed + 1 day)
AUDIENCE: every customer with a valid contact and appropriate consent for service messages
MESSAGE (email/SMS/WhatsApp):
  Hi {first_name}, thanks for choosing {business}. Would you share your honest experience?
  It helps us improve and helps others decide. It takes about a minute: {review_link}
DO NOT: offer discounts or gifts for reviews on platforms that forbid it; ask only happy customers;
        pre-screen with "How would you rate us?" and send only 4-5 stars onward (review gating).
```

**3. Respond to every review within a set time.** AI assistants can draft replies from your guidelines, but a person must check facts and tone and must never reveal private customer details:

```text
Draft a reply to this <platform> review for <business>. Tone: warm, professional, concise (under 80 words).
If negative: acknowledge, apologize where appropriate, no arguing, invite them to contact <channel>
to resolve, sign with a real name and role. Never mention order details, health or personal data.
Do not offer compensation in the public reply. Review: "<paste>"
```

**4. Monitor and report.** Track rating, volume and themes monthly. Report suspected fake or policy-violating reviews through each platform's own process (Google provides a review management tool for Business Profile owners to report and track reviews), with evidence, and never accuse reviewers publicly.

```text
REVIEW LOG
Month | Platform | New reviews | Avg rating | Response rate | Median response time | Top 3 themes | Reported (n) | Actions taken
```

### Reputation in AI answers

AI assistants and answer engines increasingly summarize what people say about a business, drawing on reviews, forums and coverage. You can't control those summaries directly, but the fundamentals apply: fix the real problems customers mention, respond publicly and helpfully, keep official profiles accurate, and earn genuine coverage. Module 4 covers how to monitor what AI answers say about your brand.

### How to measure success

Track review volume and velocity, average rating, response rate and time, the share of reviews mentioning the issues you've fixed, and brand-SERP quality (what appears on page one for your brand name). Watch complaint volume alongside ratings; a rising rating with rising complaints suggests something is wrong with how reviews are being collected.

All three break platform rules, and two of them now clearly break consumer law in the US and the UK. In this lecture, you'll learn the rules on reviews in twenty twenty-six, how to build a compliant review program, how to respond to good and bad reviews, how to manage your brand's search results, and how to prepare for a crisis.

lessons.title: Entities and brand signals
lessons.body:
### From strings to things

Modern search engines understand the web in terms of **entities** — people, organizations, places, products, concepts — and the relationships between them. Google's Knowledge Graph is a database of entities and facts. When Google confidently understands that your brand is a distinct entity (with a name, logo, founders, location, industry and official profiles), it can connect mentions across the web to you, show knowledge panels, and interpret your content in context.

### Why entity clarity matters for SEO and PR

- **Disambiguation**: "Optimize All" the agency vs a generic phrase; "Noor" the brand vs the name. Clear signals help search engines attribute mentions correctly.
- **Knowledge panels and rich brand SERPs**.
- **Attribution of coverage**: unlinked mentions still contribute to recognition when the entity is clear.
- **AI search**: answer engines rely on entity understanding to decide which brands to mention (see the AI Search course).

### Building consistent entity signals

1. **Canonical name**: choose one official brand name and use it consistently (including capitalization and spacing). Note legal names and common variants.
2. **Official website as the hub**: a thorough About page with founding date, founders, leadership, location, what you do, and links to official profiles.
3. **Organization structured data** with a stable `@id`, logo, `sameAs` links to official profiles, contact points and address where relevant:

```json
{
  "@context": "https://schema.org",
  "@type": "Organization",
  "@id": "https://www.example.com/#organization",
  "name": "Example Studio",
  "legalName": "Example Studio FZ-LLC",
  "url": "https://www.example.com/",
  "logo": "https://www.example.com/assets/logo.png",
  "foundingDate": "2019",
  "founder": {"@type": "Person", "@id": "https://www.example.com/team/sara-ahmed#person", "name": "Sara Ahmed"},
  "sameAs": [
    "https://www.linkedin.com/company/example-studio",
    "https://www.instagram.com/examplestudio",
    "https://www.youtube.com/@examplestudio"
  ]
}
```

4. **Consistent profiles**: same name, logo, description and website link on LinkedIn, social platforms, industry directories, business registries, app stores and review sites.
5. **Third-party corroboration**: coverage in reputable publications, industry associations, awards, conference speaker pages. Independent sources confirm facts better than self-description.
6. **People entities**: founders and experts with consistent bios, headshots and profile links; `Person` markup on author pages.

### Wikipedia and Wikidata: proceed with care

Wikipedia and Wikidata are influential sources for knowledge graphs, but:

- **Wikipedia notability**: an article requires significant coverage in reliable, independent sources. Most small businesses do not meet it.
- **Conflict of interest**: Wikipedia's guidelines strongly discourage editing articles about yourself or your clients, and paid editing requires disclosure under its terms of use. Undisclosed paid editing can lead to deletion and reputational damage.
- **Wikidata** has its own notability criteria; entries should be factual and referenced.

The ethical route is to **earn** coverage that makes the brand notable, and let independent editors write about it.

### Brand mentions as signals

Google has patents and statements suggesting it can recognize brand mentions and entity references without links, but it does not publish how, or how much, unlinked mentions affect ranking. Treat unlinked mentions as valuable for **brand awareness, entity understanding and AI visibility**, without claiming a precise ranking effect.

### Branded search demand

As PR and thought leadership raise awareness, more people search for your brand by name, sometimes combined with topics ("Optimize All technical SEO course"). Branded demand is a strong business signal and is easy to track in Search Console. It also makes your brand SERP more important to manage.

### An entity audit checklist

- [ ] One consistent brand name across site, profiles and citations
- [ ] About page with founders, history, location and profile links
- [ ] Organization (and Person) structured data with @id and sameAs
- [ ] Official social and directory profiles claimed, consistent and linked from the site
- [ ] Logo consistent and marked up
- [ ] Coverage in independent reputable sources
- [ ] Brand SERP reviewed: what appears, what's missing, any confusion with other entities

### Common mistakes

- Several name variants used interchangeably.
- sameAs links to profiles you do not control or that are abandoned.
- Creating a self-promotional Wikipedia article.
- Claiming precise ranking gains from unlinked mentions.

### Hands-on: validate and ship your Organization markup

1. **Draft the JSON-LD** using the example above, with your real canonical name, logo URL, founding date and only the profiles you control.
2. **Add Person markup** for founders and key experts on their profile pages, each with its own stable `@id` (for example `https://www.example.com/team/sara-ahmed#person`), and reference those `@id`s from the Organization (`founder`, `employee`) and from articles (`author`).
3. **Validate.** Paste the page URL or code into the Schema Markup Validator (validator.schema.org) to check syntax, and use Google's Rich Results Test to confirm Google can read the page. Organization markup doesn't produce a rich result on its own, but the test still shows parsing errors.
4. **Place it once.** Add the Organization block to the homepage or About page (many sites add it site-wide via the template); avoid multiple conflicting versions.
5. **Audit profiles against the markup.** Every `sameAs` URL should be a live, official profile that uses the same name, logo and description.

```text
ENTITY CONSISTENCY SHEET
Property          | Website (About) | LinkedIn | Instagram | YouTube | Google Business Profile | Directory X | Wikidata (if any)
Name (exact)      |                 |          |           |         |                         |             |
Logo (same file?) |                 |          |           |         |                         |             |
Short description |                 |          |           |         |                         |             |
Founded / HQ      |                 |          |           |         |                         |             |
Website link      |                 |          |           |         |                         |             |
Action needed     |                 |          |           |         |                         |             |
```

### Tracking branded search demand

Search Console's Performance report now includes a **branded queries filter** (introduced in late 2025 and available to eligible sites — generally top-level properties with enough query volume), which separates branded from non-branded queries automatically. If it isn't available for your property, use a regex filter on queries instead, for example:

```text
Query filter → Custom (regex) → Matches regex:
(?i)(optimi[sz]e ?all|optimizeall|optimize all)
```

Include common misspellings and transliterations (for example English and Arabic spellings of the brand), and compare branded impressions month over month and year over year.

### Entities and AI answers

AI answer engines need to identify which entity a mention refers to before they can describe or recommend it. Consistent names, a clear About page, structured data that ties official profiles together and independent coverage all reduce ambiguity. The last lesson in this module covers how to see and measure what AI answers say about your brand.

### How to measure success

Track the number of inconsistencies fixed on your consistency sheet, validation errors (zero), branded impressions and clicks in Search Console, and whether the brand SERP shows the right site, profiles and (where one exists) knowledge panel without confusion with other entities.

lessons.title: E-E-A-T, author pages and quality signals
lessons.body:
### What E-E-A-T is

**E-E-A-T** stands for **Experience, Expertise, Authoritativeness and Trust**. It comes from Google's **Search Quality Rater Guidelines**, used by human raters who evaluate search results to help Google test and improve its systems. Key points:

- E-E-A-T is a **framework for assessing quality**, not a single ranking factor or score. Google has said its systems use a mix of signals that align with what raters would consider E-E-A-T.
- **Trust** is the most important element; experience, expertise and authoritativeness support it.
- The bar is highest for **YMYL (Your Money or Your Life)** topics — health, finance, safety, legal, civic information — where poor content could harm people.

### The four components

| Component | Question | Evidence examples |
|---|---|---|
| **Experience** | Has the creator actually used, done or lived this? | First-hand photos, original test results, "we tried it for three months" details, case studies |
| **Expertise** | Does the creator have the knowledge or skill? | Qualifications, professional role, track record, depth and accuracy |
| **Authoritativeness** | Is the creator or site a go-to source? | Citations by others, reputable coverage, industry recognition |
| **Trust** | Is the page accurate, honest, safe and reliable? | Clear sourcing, transparency about who is behind it, secure checkout, policies, corrections |

### Google's "Who, How, Why" questions

Google's guidance on helpful content suggests asking:

- **Who** created the content? Make it self-evident — bylines, author pages.
- **How** was it created? Explain methodology, testing, and where appropriate, how automation or AI was used.
- **Why** was it created? Primarily to help people, not to manipulate rankings.

Using AI to help create content is not against Google's guidelines; using automation primarily to manipulate rankings (scaled content abuse) is. Where readers would reasonably expect to know how content was produced, disclosure helps trust.

### Author pages that work

For every author and expert:

```text
/team/sara-ahmed/
- Name, headshot, role
```

Add `Person` structured data and reference it from articles:

```json
{
  "@context": "https://schema.org",
  "@type": "Article",
  "headline": "How to plan a hreflang rollout for a bilingual store",
  "author": {
    "@type": "Person",
    "@id": "https://www.example.com/team/sara-ahmed#person",
    "name": "Sara Ahmed",
    "url": "https://www.example.com/team/sara-ahmed/",
    "jobTitle": "Head of Technical SEO",
    "sameAs": ["https://www.linkedin.com/in/example-sara-ahmed"]
  },
  "publisher": {"@id": "https://www.example.com/#organization"},
  "datePublished": "2026-02-10",
  "dateModified": "2026-03-01"
}
```

Markup does not create expertise; it describes it. The underlying reality — real experts, real experience — is what matters.

### Site-level trust signals

- **About page** with the real people and organization behind the site.
- **Contact information** that works (address, phone, email appropriate to the business).
- **Editorial policy**: how content is researched, reviewed, updated and corrected.
- **Review process for YMYL**: e.g. "Medically reviewed by Dr. ..." — only if genuinely done.
- **Customer service and policies**: returns, shipping, privacy, terms — especially for e-commerce.
- **Transparent monetization**: affiliate disclosures, sponsored content labels.
- **Accuracy**: cite sources, update outdated content, show dates honestly.

### Off-site E-E-A-T

Raters are asked to look for independent information about a site and its creators: news coverage, reviews, awards, professional bodies, Wikipedia where applicable. This is where digital PR, thought leadership and reputation management directly support quality perception.

### An E-E-A-T review for a page

1. Is the author clear, and are their experience and expertise evident and verifiable?
2. Does the content show first-hand experience (original photos, data, examples)?
3. Are claims sourced and accurate? Are dates honest?
4. Is the purpose to help the reader, with commercial intent transparent?
5. Would the site be trusted by someone checking independent reviews and coverage?
6. For YMYL, is there appropriate expert review?

### Common mistakes

- Fake author personas or stock-photo "experts".
- Adding "reviewed by" labels without real review.
- Updating the date without updating the content.
- Treating E-E-A-T as a checklist of schema tags.

### Hands-on: an author page and byline system that proves "who"

**1. Build one profile page per author or expert**, following the structure above, at a stable URL (`/team/sara-ahmed/`). Include a real headshot, specific experience, verifiable credentials and links to official profiles.

**2. Add a consistent byline block to every article**, linking to the profile page:

```text
By Sara Ahmed, Head of Technical SEO — 12 years running technical SEO for retail sites
Reviewed by Dr. Omar Khalid, Data Protection Counsel (for articles on privacy law) — only if a genuine review happened
Published: 2026-02-10 · Updated: 2026-03-01 (what changed: updated screenshots and the Q1 data)
```

**3. Mark it up.** Reference the Person `@id` from each Article's `author`, and the Organization `@id` as `publisher` (see the example above). Keep one Person entity per real person across the site.

**4. Publish an editorial policy page** describing how content is researched, who reviews it (especially for YMYL topics), how AI tools are used, how corrections work and how often content is reviewed.

```text
EDITORIAL POLICY (outline)
Who writes: named staff experts and vetted contributors (bios linked)
How we research: primary sources, original testing/data; sources cited in-text
Expert review: YMYL articles reviewed by a qualified professional before publishing
Use of AI: we use AI tools to help with research summaries, outlines and editing; every article is
           written or substantially edited, fact-checked and approved by a named author
Corrections: email <address>; corrections noted at the end of the article with date
Updates: key articles reviewed at least every 12 months; "Updated" date changes only with real changes
```

### A quick E-E-A-T gap audit with an AI assistant

You can ask an AI assistant to compare a page against Google's "Who, How, Why" questions. It can't verify credentials or experience, so use it to find gaps, then fill them with real evidence:

```text
Review this article (pasted) and its author box. Using Google's "Who, How, Why" questions for helpful
content, list what a skeptical reader could NOT verify: who wrote it and why they're qualified, how the
information was produced (testing, data, sources), and why it exists. Suggest specific evidence to add.
Do not invent credentials or claims.
```

### How to measure success

Track the share of articles with a named author linked to a complete profile, YMYL articles with documented expert review, pages with accurate "updated" dates, and — over time — branded and author-name searches, citations of your experts, and the performance of your most important informational pages after quality improvements.
