lessons.body:
### A new place where reputation shows up

People increasingly ask AI assistants and AI search features questions that used to start with a search box: "best accounting software for a small business in the UAE", "is this brand legit?", "which agencies in Lahore do technical SEO?". The answers name some brands and not others, describe them in particular ways, and sometimes cite sources. For digital PR, this is a new surface where coverage, reviews and entity clarity pay off — and where you need a way to measure what's happening.

### How AI answers are assembled (simplified)

| System | How it tends to draw on the web |
|---|---|
| Google AI Overviews and AI Mode | Built on Google Search's ranking and quality systems; show supporting links to indexed pages |
| ChatGPT (with search), Perplexity, Microsoft Copilot, Gemini | Combine the model's training with live web retrieval for many queries; often show cited sources |
| Assistants without browsing | Rely on training data, which reflects what was widely written about you before the model's cutoff |

Two consequences follow. First, much of what appears depends on what reputable, independent sources on the web say about you — the same sources digital PR targets. Second, answers vary between runs, users, locations and products, so single screenshots prove little. You need systematic sampling.

### What Google says (2025–2026)

Google's Search Central documentation on AI features states there are no additional requirements or special optimizations to appear in AI Overviews or AI Mode beyond being indexed and eligible to show with a snippet, and that normal SEO best practices apply. In May 2026 Google published a guide to optimizing for generative AI features on Google Search that reiterates this: generative features are rooted in core ranking and quality systems, `llms.txt` files receive no special treatment, and there's no need to break content into artificial chunks. In June 2026 Search Console began showing **generative AI performance reports** (impressions for AI Overviews, AI Mode and generative features in Discover, by page, country, device and date), rolled out to all websites by the end of August 2026; at launch they did not include clicks or query data. Check current documentation, because these reports are evolving.

### What actually moves AI visibility

1. **Be clearly identifiable** (previous lessons): one canonical name, About page, Organization markup, consistent profiles.
2. **Be described by independent, reputable sources** — coverage, trade press, expert commentary, reviews, industry lists and comparisons written by others.
3. **Publish specific, citable, non-commodity content** — original data, clear pricing and product facts, methodology, expert explanations that others can't copy.
4. **Fix real reputation problems** — AI summaries often reflect recurring complaints in reviews and forums.
5. **Keep facts consistent** everywhere (pricing, locations, founding details), so systems don't pick up outdated information.

Avoid tactics that try to manipulate AI answers, such as mass-publishing self-promotional "best X" lists across low-quality sites, fake reviews or hidden instructions to AI systems. They risk spam-policy violations and reputational damage, and they tend not to last.

### Hands-on: build an AI visibility sampling panel

**1. Write 20–40 prompts** your customers would realistically ask, across stages: category ("best payroll software for small businesses in Saudi Arabia"), comparison ("X vs Y for freelancers"), and brand ("is BrandName reliable?"). Include local languages where relevant.

**2. Sample systematically.** Once a month, run each prompt in the AI products your audience uses (for example Google AI Mode or AI Overviews where available, ChatGPT, Perplexity, Gemini, Copilot), logged out or in a clean profile, from the relevant country where possible. Run the key prompts more than once, because answers vary. Record results in a CSV:

```text
date,engine,country,prompt_id,prompt,run,answer_text,cited_urls
2026-09-02,perplexity,AE,p07,"best payroll software for small businesses in the UAE",1,"...","https://...;https://..."
```

Commercial tools can automate parts of this (for example Ahrefs Brand Radar and Semrush's AI visibility toolkit track mentions and citations across several AI products). Check coverage of your markets and languages before relying on any tool.

**3. Analyze with Python.**

```python
# pip install pandas
import re
import pandas as pd
from urllib.parse import urlparse

BRANDS = {
    "our_brand": [r"\bexample payroll\b", r"\bexamplepay\b"],
    "competitor_a": [r"\bcompetitor a\b"],
    "competitor_b": [r"\bcompetitor b\b"],
}

df = pd.read_csv("ai_answers.csv")
df["answer_text"] = df["answer_text"].fillna("").str.lower()

for brand, patterns in BRANDS.items():
    rx = re.compile("|".join(patterns), re.I)
    df[brand] = df["answer_text"].apply(lambda t: bool(rx.search(t)))

mention_rate = df.groupby("engine")[list(BRANDS)].mean().round(2)       # share of answers mentioning each brand
share_of_voice = df[list(BRANDS)].sum() / df[list(BRANDS)].sum().sum()  # among all brand mentions
print("Mention rate by engine:\n", mention_rate)
print("\nShare of voice:\n", share_of_voice.round(2))

def domains(cell: str) -> list[str]:
    return [urlparse(u.strip()).netloc.removeprefix("www.") for u in str(cell).split(";") if u.strip()]

cited = df["cited_urls"].apply(domains).explode().dropna()
print("\nMost-cited domains:\n", cited.value_counts().head(15))
```

The most-cited domains list is your PR target list: publications, directories, review sites and forums that AI answers lean on for your category.

**4. Act on the findings.** If answers describe you inaccurately, fix the facts at the source (your site, profiles, directories). If competitors are named from particular publications, pitch those publications with genuinely useful stories. If complaints dominate, fix the underlying issue and respond publicly.

### Worked example: a payroll software startup in Riyadh

A startup samples 30 prompts monthly across four AI products. Month one: it appears in few category answers, while two competitors appear often, typically citing a regional tech publication and a software review site. Brand prompts return outdated pricing from an old directory listing. The team corrects the directory, publishes clear pricing and a methodology-backed salary data report, earns coverage in the regional tech publication, and runs a compliant review program. Over the next two quarters, its mention rate in category prompts rises and brand answers show current pricing. (Illustrative scenario.)

### How to measure success

Report mention rate and share of voice by engine and prompt group, accuracy of brand descriptions (a simple correct/partly/incorrect score), the domains cited for your category, and Search Console's generative AI impressions for your key pages. Treat changes over months, not single runs, as signal.

lessons.title: Knowledge panels: earning and managing them
lessons.body:
### What a knowledge panel is

A knowledge panel is the information box Google shows for entities it understands well — organizations, people, places, works. It draws on the Knowledge Graph, which is built from many sources: the entity's own website, structured data, licensed data, public sources such as Wikipedia and Wikidata, and other reputable websites. Local businesses see a different feature — the **Google Business Profile** panel — which is managed separately (see the Local SEO course).

You **cannot buy or directly create** a knowledge panel. Google generates it automatically when it has enough confidence about an entity and there is search demand for it.

### Why panels matter

- They dominate the brand SERP on desktop and show prominently on mobile.
- They present facts (founders, founding date, social profiles) that users trust.
- They indicate that Google understands the entity — a foundation for accurate representation in AI features too.

### Factors that make a panel more likely

Google does not publish a formula, but practitioners observe that panels are more likely when:

1. **The entity is clearly defined** on its official site (About page, Organization/Person markup, consistent name).
2. **Independent reputable sources** describe the entity consistently — news coverage, industry bodies, reference sites.
3. **Official profiles** are consistent and interlinked (sameAs).
4. **There is search demand** for the name.
5. **For people**: a consistent public presence — author pages, speaker bios, interviews, books, professional listings.

Treat this as a set of good practices that also help brand understanding generally — not a guaranteed trigger.

### Claiming a knowledge panel

If a panel exists for you or your organization, you can request verification through Google's process ("Get verified on Google" / claiming the panel). Typically you sign in with an account associated with an official presence (for example, the official website in Search Console, or official social or YouTube accounts) and follow the verification steps. Once verified you can:

- **Suggest changes** to facts (which Google reviews, often requiring supporting sources).
- **Suggest a featured image** from available options in some cases.
- **Receive updates** about the panel.

Anyone can also use the **Feedback** link on a panel to report inaccuracies, but verified representatives' suggestions carry more weight.

### Correcting wrong information

1. Identify the source of the error — often a third-party site or an outdated profile.
2. Fix it at the source where possible (update your About page, profiles, Wikidata entry via proper processes, press bios).
3. Submit a suggested edit through the panel (verified or feedback), citing authoritative sources.
4. Be patient; changes are reviewed and can take weeks.

### Person panels for experts and founders

For thought leaders, a person panel reinforces credibility. Supportive actions:

- A detailed author/founder page on the company site with Person markup and sameAs to official profiles.
- Consistent name (including transliteration choices — for example, Muhammad vs Mohammed — pick one publicly and use it everywhere).
- Speaker pages, interviews, podcast show notes and bylines with consistent bios.
- Where genuinely notable, independent coverage in reputable outlets.

### Ethical boundaries

- Do not fabricate awards, credentials or press mentions to build a panel.
- Avoid paid "knowledge panel creation" services that rely on low-quality press releases, fake profiles or undisclosed Wikipedia edits — they may produce short-lived results and reputational risk.
- Keep facts accurate: panels displaying false information about founders or dates are embarrassing and hard to fix.

### Monitoring

Search the brand and key people monthly (logged out, and from different locations or with a SERP localization tool). Check the panel's facts, images and social links. After rebrands, leadership changes or moves, update the website and profiles first, then suggest panel edits.

### Common mistakes

- Confusing Google Business Profile management with knowledge panel management.
- Trying to "create" a panel via mass press release distribution.
- Using different name spellings across profiles.

### Hands-on: a knowledge panel audit and claim workflow

**1. Check what exists.** Search the brand and each key person in a private window, from the main markets you serve (use a VPN or a SERP localization tool if needed, and check the local-language spelling too). Record whether a panel appears, which facts it shows and which sources it seems to draw on.

```text
KNOWLEDGE PANEL AUDIT
Entity: __________  Type: Organization / Person   Markets checked: __________
Panel present? Y/N   Title shown: __________   Subtitle/description: __________
Facts shown (founded, founders, HQ, CEO, etc.) + apparent source: __________
Images and social profiles shown: __________
Errors or outdated facts: __________     Source of error (if identifiable): __________
Action: fix at source / suggest edit / build signals / none      Owner: ______  Date: ______
```

**2. Claim it (if a panel exists).** On the panel, use the option to claim it (often shown as "Claim this knowledge panel"), then follow Google's verification steps, which typically involve signing in with an account connected to an official presence such as the website's Search Console property or an official YouTube or social account. Verification steps change over time; follow the current instructions on Google's help pages.

**3. Correct errors at the source first.** Update your About page, Organization/Person markup, official profiles and any directory or reference listing (including Wikidata, following its sourcing rules) before suggesting edits in the panel, and cite authoritative sources in your suggestions.

**4. Build signals if no panel exists yet.** Revisit the entity consistency sheet from Module 4, strengthen author and founder pages, and earn independent coverage that describes the entity consistently. There is no guaranteed trigger.

### Knowledge panels and AI answers

The same entity understanding that powers knowledge panels also helps AI features describe your brand accurately. After a rebrand, leadership change or move, update your site and profiles first, then check both the panel and your AI visibility sampling panel (previous module) over the following weeks.

### How to measure success

Track panel presence for the brand and key people, the number of factual errors outstanding, time to correct errors after changes, and whether the brand SERP and sampled AI answers show consistent, current facts.

lessons.title: Measuring digital PR and brand authority
lessons.body:
### Measure what the business values

Digital PR sits between SEO, communications and brand. Good measurement speaks to all three without inflating results.

### Avoid vanity measures

- **Advertising Value Equivalency (AVE)** — the cost of buying equivalent ad space — is widely rejected by the communications industry (the Barcelona Principles, maintained by the measurement body AMEC, explicitly reject AVEs as a measure of communication value).
- **"Potential reach"** totals (sum of publications' audiences) wildly overstate actual exposure.
- **Third-party authority score changes** alone say little about business impact.

### A balanced scorecard

**Coverage quality**

| Metric | How |
|---|---|
| Coverage count by tier | Define tiers: Tier 1 (national/top trade), Tier 2 (regional/major niche), Tier 3 (blogs/aggregators) |
| Relevance | Share of coverage in outlets your customers read |
| Message pull-through | Did coverage include the key message, brand name, spokesperson? |
| Sentiment | Positive/neutral/negative, assessed by a human |

**Search and site impact**

| Metric | How |
|---|---|
| Links earned | New linking domains, followed/nofollow split, link targets |
| Referral traffic and conversions | GA4 traffic acquisition by source |
| Branded search demand | Search Console branded query impressions and clicks over time |
| Target page performance | Impressions/clicks for topic pages supported by the campaign |
| Brand SERP quality | Panel presence, positive results in the top ten |

**Brand and business**

| Metric | How |
|---|---|
| Share of voice | Your mentions vs competitors' in target media over a period |
| Inbound requests | Journalist inquiries, speaking and podcast invitations |
| Sales influence | Leads citing coverage; sales team feedback |
| AI visibility | Whether AI assistants mention or cite the brand for key topics (manual sampling; measurement tools are immature) |

### Setting baselines and targets

Before a campaign: capture branded search levels, referring domains, share of voice, and brand SERP state. Set targets as ranges and directions ("increase Tier 1–2 coverage in UAE business media; grow branded impressions year-over-year") rather than fixed promises.

### Reporting cadence

- **Campaign reports** two to four weeks after launch: coverage list, links, referral traffic, highlights, lessons.
- **Monthly program reports**: cumulative results, reactive PR wins, pipeline.
- **Quarterly reviews**: branded demand, share of voice, business outcomes, strategic adjustments.

### A campaign report template

```text
Campaign: [Name]  Launch: [date]  Markets: UAE, KSA, UK
Summary: 3 lines on outcome and what we learned

Coverage: [n] pieces — Tier 1: [n], Tier 2: [n], Tier 3: [n]
Highlights: [outlet, headline, link, whether it links]
Links: [n] new linking domains ([n] followed); top links listed
Traffic: [n] referral sessions; [n] conversions (GA4)
Brand: branded impressions [change vs prior period and YoY]
Messages: key message present in [x of y] articles
Lessons: angles that worked; outlets to prioritize; what we'd change
Next: follow-up pitches, localized angles, relationship notes
```

### Attribution honesty

Brand growth has many causes: advertising, product launches, seasonality, word of mouth. When you report changes in branded search or organic traffic, note concurrent activities. Where possible, compare markets that received the campaign with those that did not.

### Tools

Media monitoring platforms, Google Alerts for lightweight monitoring, backlink tools, Search Console, GA4, and a simple spreadsheet or BI dashboard for share-of-voice tracking. Choose tools that cover your languages and markets — Arabic and Urdu media coverage is poorly tracked by some tools, so supplement with manual monitoring.

### Common mistakes

- Reporting AVE or potential reach as value.
- Counting syndicated copies of one article as separate coverage wins.
- Only reporting links, ignoring brand and business outcomes.
- Using tools that miss non-English coverage in your markets.

### Barcelona Principles 4.0 (2025)

In 2025 AMEC (the International Association for the Measurement and Evaluation of Communication) published **Barcelona Principles 4.0**, updating the industry's measurement standard. The update keeps the seven-principle structure, continues to reject AVEs as a measure of value, and puts stronger emphasis on outcomes and impact, stakeholder-focused measurement, and ethics, governance and transparency with data, methods and AI. It links more clearly to AMEC's Integrated Evaluation Framework. If you report to communications leaders, align your scorecard language with it.

### Hands-on: build the scorecard data pipeline

**1. Search Console.** Use the Performance report's branded queries filter (or a regex filter) to export branded impressions and clicks monthly, and the page filter for campaign landing pages. In 2026 Search Console also began reporting impressions in generative AI features (AI Overviews, AI Mode and Discover); export these for campaign pages where available.

**2. GA4.** Tag every link you control in pitches, press kits and newsroom pages with UTM parameters, and track referrals from coverage:

```text
https://www.example.com/research/rent-index?utm_source=press_kit&utm_medium=pr&utm_campaign=rent_index_2026
GA4: Reports → Acquisition → Traffic acquisition → filter Session source contains the outlet domains;
     compare key events (e.g., generate_lead) from referral traffic in the campaign period.
```

**3. Coverage log.** One row per unique article (not per syndicated copy):

```text
Date | Outlet | Tier | Country/Language | Headline | URL | Syndication of (if any) | Link (followed/nofollow/sponsored/none) |
Link target | Key message present? | Spokesperson named? | Sentiment (human) | Campaign
```

**4. Share of voice.** Count your mentions versus named competitors in your target outlets over a period (from your monitoring tool, supplemented with manual Arabic/Urdu searches), and add AI share of voice from your sampling panel.

**5. A simple Python roll-up** turns the coverage log into campaign numbers:

```python
import pandas as pd

log = pd.read_csv("coverage_log.csv")
unique = log[log["Syndication of (if any)"].isna()]                 # exclude syndicated copies
summary = unique.groupby("Campaign").agg(
    pieces=("URL", "count"),
    tier1=("Tier", lambda t: (t == 1).sum()),
    followed_links=("Link (followed/nofollow/sponsored/none)", lambda s: (s == "followed").sum()),
    message_pull_through=("Key message present?", lambda s: (s == "Y").mean().round(2)),
)
print(summary.to_string())
```

### How to measure success

A good measurement setup lets you answer, within a day of a request: what did this campaign earn (coverage by tier, links, messages), what did it do (referrals, conversions, branded demand, AI visibility), and what did we learn? Review the scorecard quarterly with the same definitions, so trends are comparable.

lessons.body:
### Where AI genuinely helps in digital PR

Used well, AI assistants and APIs remove the slowest, most repetitive parts of PR work so people can spend more time on judgment, relationships and real expertise. Used badly, they produce the generic, inaccurate pitches journalists now delete on sight. This lesson gives you workflows that help, with the guardrails that keep your credibility intact.

| Task | Good AI use | Human must |
|---|---|---|
| Ideation | Generate and critique angles; play a skeptical editor | Choose ideas; validate against real data and coverage |
| Research | Summarize long reports, regulations or datasets you provide | Read primary sources; check every figure |
| Media lists | Summarize a journalist's recent articles you've pasted, to suggest an angle | Verify beats and contacts from the outlet itself |
| Pitch drafting | Draft from a verified fact sheet; adapt tone per segment | Personalize, fact-check, send from a real person |
| Reactive PR | Turn expert voice notes into a first draft | Ensure quotes are the expert's own approved words |
| Coverage analysis | Classify message pull-through and themes across many articles | Spot-check classifications; judge sentiment |
| Reporting | Draft summaries from your scorecard data | Check every number; add context and lessons |

Never let AI invent statistics, quotes, credentials, journalists' interests or coverage. Language models can generate plausible text that isn't true.

### Guardrails for AI in PR

1. **Verified inputs only.** Feed models fact sheets, transcripts and articles you've checked; ask them to mark gaps rather than fill them.
2. **Named humans own outputs.** Every pitch, quote and report has a person accountable for its accuracy.
3. **Privacy.** Use business accounts or APIs with appropriate data-handling terms; don't paste customer personal data or confidential deal information into tools your organization hasn't approved. Journalists' public work details (name, outlet, beat, published articles) are different from private personal data, but data-protection law (for example GDPR/UK GDPR) still applies to how you store and use contact lists.
4. **Honesty about AI use** where a platform, publication or journalist asks, and in your editorial policy.
5. **No mass personalization theater.** A merge field that says "I loved your recent article" is worse than no personalization.

### Hands-on: a coverage analyzer with the Anthropic API (Python)

This script classifies each coverage excerpt for message pull-through and spokesperson mention, returning JSON you can add to your coverage log. It reads the API key and model name from environment variables — never hard-code keys — and handles errors. Check Anthropic's current documentation for model names and SDK details.

```python
# pip install anthropic pandas
import json
import os
import sys

import anthropic
import pandas as pd

MODEL = os.environ.get("ANTHROPIC_MODEL")          # set to a current model from the docs
if not MODEL or not os.environ.get("ANTHROPIC_API_KEY"):
    sys.exit("Set ANTHROPIC_API_KEY and ANTHROPIC_MODEL environment variables.")

client = anthropic.Anthropic()                       # reads ANTHROPIC_API_KEY

KEY_MESSAGES = [
    "Rents rose faster than salaries for young workers in most cities studied",
    "The index uses official rent and earnings data",
]
SPOKESPERSON = "Dr. Faisal Rahman"

SYSTEM = ("You classify news coverage for a PR measurement log. Use only the text provided. "
          "Return strict JSON with keys: key_messages_present (list of indices), spokesperson_named (true/false), "
          "brand_described_accurately (yes/partly/no/unclear), evidence (short verbatim quotes). "
          "If unsure, say 'unclear'. Never infer facts not in the text.")

def classify(excerpt: str) -> dict:
    prompt = (f"Key messages (indexed): {json.dumps(KEY_MESSAGES)}\n"
              f"Spokesperson: {SPOKESPERSON}\n\nCoverage excerpt:\n\"\"\"{excerpt}\"\"\"")
    try:
        resp = client.messages.create(
            model=MODEL, max_tokens=500, system=SYSTEM,
            messages=[{"role": "user", "content": prompt}],
        )
    except anthropic.APIError as e:
        return {"error": f"API error: {e}"}
    text = "".join(block.text for block in resp.content if block.type == "text")
    try:
        return json.loads(text)
    except json.JSONDecodeError:
        return {"error": "Non-JSON response", "raw": text[:300]}

log = pd.read_csv("coverage_excerpts.csv")           # columns: url, outlet, excerpt
results = [classify(x) for x in log["excerpt"].fillna("")]
log["ai_classification"] = [json.dumps(r) for r in results]
log.to_csv("coverage_classified.csv", index=False)
print(f"Classified {len(log)} items. Spot-check at least 20% by hand before reporting.")
```

Spot-check a sample by hand before any number goes into a report, and keep sentiment judgments human.

### Hands-on: a pitch personalization prompt that can't invent

```text
You help a PR professional personalize a pitch. Below are (A) our verified fact sheet and
(B) the text of the journalist's two most recent relevant articles (pasted from the outlet).
Write ONE opening sentence connecting our story to something specific in (B), and suggest which
of our findings in (A) fits their coverage best. If nothing in (B) genuinely connects, say
"No strong connection — consider another journalist." Do not invent facts about the journalist or us.
(A) <fact sheet>
(B) <article texts>
```

### Worked example: a four-person PR team's AI workflow

An agency in Dubai uses AI to summarize regulations for its reactive program, to draft pitches from verified fact sheets, and to classify coverage for monthly reports. It keeps three rules: every quote comes from a named expert's approved words, every pitch is personalized and sent by a named person, and every report number is spot-checked. The time saved goes into more calls with journalists and better data — which is where coverage actually comes from. (Illustrative scenario.)

### How to measure success

Compare before and after on the things that matter: time from news break to response, pitches sent per piece of coverage, journalist reply rates, error rates found in spot-checks (they should be low and falling), and hours freed for relationship work and research.

scenes.narration: A word on privacy and tools, because this is where well-meaning teams get into trouble. Use business accounts or APIs with data-handling terms your organization has approved, and check whether inputs may be used for training. Don't paste customer personal data, confidential deal details or unreleased results into consumer chat tools. Media lists are personal data too, even when they only hold a journalist's work email and beat, so store them securely, use them for relevant professional contact, and honor opt-outs quickly, in line with laws like GDPR and UK GDPR. And keep a short note in your editorial policy explaining how your team uses AI. If a journalist or platform asks, answer honestly.

Time from news break to response. Pitches sent per piece of coverage. Journalist reply rates. Error rates found in spot-checks, which should be low and falling. And hours freed for relationships and research.
